What we’ll cover

  1. How to model dichotomous dependent variables (voted, didn’t vote; war, no war; democracy, autocracy etc.)

  2. The linear probability model and its flaws.

The Linear Probability Model

The Linear Probability Model

  • Using linear regression (OLS) on a dichotomous dependent variable will give us a Linear Probability Model.

  • We’ll talk about the problems with this approach.

A simple turnout model

  • I want to model individual voter turnout.

  • My first model just uses a dummy variable to indicate whether a person has a college degree (1= degree, 0 = no degree)

  • My DV is a dummy for whether a respondent voted in 2020 that equals 1 if a person voted and 0 otherwise.

  • In essence, I’m predicting the probability of voting \(Pr(y=1)\) as a function of education.

Code 
nes$turnout_dummy<-transformC(type='dummy', 
           x=turnout2020, 
           data=nes, 
           response = '1. Voted',
           confirm=FALSE
           )

nes$bachelors_or_more <- transformC(type = 'dummy', 
                                    x = educ.5cat,
                                    data= nes,
                                    response = c("4. Bachelor's degree", "5. Graduate degree"),
                                    confirm =FALSE
                                    )

Linear probability model

  • We can interpret LPM coefficients as the effect of a one unit increase in X on the probability of Y=1.

  • The LPM is fine for a single dichotomous IV, but we can run into issues when we have more complex models.

Linear probability model

For example: I have a more complex model that includes a respondent’s total number correct on 10 political knowledge questions:

Code 
# getting total correct answers for all the political knowledge questions
nes$polquiz.index <- ((nes$polquiz.fedspend == "1. Foreign aid (correct)") +
                        (nes$polquiz.german == "1. Correct") +
                        (nes$polquiz.housemaj == "1. Democrats (correct)") +
                        (nes$polquiz.russian == "1. Correct") +
                        (
                          nes$polquiz.scotus == "2. Correct" |
                            nes$polquiz.scotus == "1. Partially correct"
                        ) +
                        (nes$polquiz.sen.term == 6) +
                        (nes$polquiz.senatemaj == "2. Republicans (correct)") +
                        (nes$polquiz.speaker == "1. Correct") +
                        (nes$polquiz.vp == "1. Correct")
)

Linear probability model

Code 
turnout_model_2 <- regC(turnout_dummy ~  bachelors_or_more + polquiz.index,
                       w=wt, 
                       data=nes )

turnout_model_2

So what’s the probability of turnout for a person who got all 10 political knowledge questions correct?

\(\text{Pr(turnout)} = .58 + 0.07 + 0.04 \times 10 = 1.05\)

Does this make sense?

Problems with the LPM

First the LPM can give us predictions that are above 100% or below 0% for many observations.

Problems with the LPM

Second the LPM assumes that the effect of X on Y is constant across all values of X, but this isn’t true for dichotomous outcomes.

Problems with the LPM

  • For dichotomous outcomes, most effects are strongest when someone is “on-the-fence” and weaker when they’re already nearly certain to do or not do something

  • ex: if someone always/never votes no matter what, they’re not going to be influenced by a get out the vote effort.

Problems with the LPM

Third the errors for an LPM also aren’t normally distributed, which can lead to incorrect p-values.

Linear Probability models

  • These aren’t necessarily fatal flaws, and there is a school of thought that argues that the linear probability model is basically fine for most situations. (and it’s definitely fine if we have a single dichotomous control variable.)

  • However, logistic regression is a relatively easy alternative that does a better job of modeling the way that dichotomous outcomes actually work.

Logistic Regression

Logistic Regression

Logistic regression models the effect of X on Y using a logistic function instead of a line.

\[ Pr(Y=1|X) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\alpha + \beta_1\text{x}_1+ \beta_2\text{x}_2...}} \]

Logistic Regression

  • The logistic function is an S-shaped curve that can never reach 0 or 1.

  • Its relationship to the probability of an event is non-linear, which means that the effect of a one unit change in X will not be the same at all values of X.

The Logistic function

In terms of probability, the “slope” will determine how quickly Pr(Y=1) approaches 1 or 0 as X changes.

The Logistic function

The intercept has the effect of moving the curve right or left.

Logistic Regression

  • The coefficient in a logit model represents the estimated effect of a one unit change in the independent variable on the logged-odds of the dependent variable occurring.

\[ log(\frac{p}{1-p}) = \alpha + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2X_2 ... \]

So:

  1. What are “odds”?

  2. What are “logged odds”?

What are odds?

What are odds?

You can think of the odds as a measure of how often “A” happens relative to how often “B” happens.

What are odds?

The odds of an event would be the probability of that event occurring divided by the probability of that event not occurring.

What are odds?

Getting odds from a probability:

\[ \text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p} \]

  • if the probability \(= .80\), the odds are: \(.8/.2 = 4\)
  • if the probability \(=.2\), the odds are \(.2/.8 = .25\)

Getting probabilities from odds:

\[ p = \text{odds}/(1+\text{odds}) \]

  • if the odds are 4, the probability is \(4/5 = .8\)
  • if the odds are .25, the probability is \(.25/1.25 = .2\)

What are odds?

We’ll generally think of an “effect” on odds in terms of multiplying or dividing the odds of some event:

If I claim “my get out the vote campaign quadrupled the odds of voting”, that means that a person with 4 to 1 odds would then have 16 to 1 odds.

In terms of probability, that would mean someone with an 80% chance:

\[ 4/(1+4) = .8 \]

Changing to a 94% chance:

\[ 16/(1+16) \approx .94 \]

What are odds?

In terms of probability, the effect of “quadrupling the odds of voting” will be different depending on the initial odds of voting.

Initial probability of voting Initial odds of voting New odds of voting New probability of voting Change in probability of voting
0.2 0.25 1.00 0.50 +0.3
0.4 0.67 2.67 0.73 +0.33
0.6 1.50 6.00 0.86 +0.26
0.8 4.00 16.00 0.94 +0.14

What are odds?

  • The odds of an event can range from 0 to infinity, so there’s no “maximum” like there is with a probability.
  • Changes in the odds are non-linear: the difference between p=.8 and .9, in odds, is much larger than the difference between p=.1 and .2
  • We can speak about the odds of an event “doubling” or “tripling” or “halving” instead of increasing linearly.
Probability of y = 1 Odds of y = 1
0.0 0/1 = 0
0.1 0.1/0.9 = 0.11
0.2 0.2/0.8 = 0.25
0.3 0.3/0.7 = 0.43
0.4 0.4/0.6 = 0.67
0.5 0.5/0.5 = 1
0.6 0.6/0.4 = 1.5
0.7 0.7/0.3 = 2.33
0.8 0.8/0.2 = 4
0.9 0.9/0.1 = 9
1.0 1/0 = Inf

What are logged odds?

What are logged odds?

The logged odds are the natural logarithm of the odds.

The natural logarithm is the exponent that you would need to raise Euler’s number by in order to equal some value.

\[ e \approx 2.71828... \]

\[ \ln(5) \approx 1.61 \]

\[ e^{1.61} \approx 5 \]

What are logged odds?

Logged odds range from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\)

Negative values mean \(Pr(y=1) < .5\), positive values mean \(Pr(y=1) > .5\) and 0 means \(Pr(y=1) = .5\)

What are logged odds?

Working with logarithms changes multiplication problems into addition problems. For instance, \(ln(4) + ln(4) = ln(4\times4)\)

Really!

log(4) + log(4)
[1] 2.772589
log(16)
[1] 2.772589

What are logged odds?

This ability to transform multiplication problems into addition is important, because it lets us express non-linear relationships in linear terms.

What are logged odds?

Notice that the odds of \(y=1\) are (approximately) quadrupling, but the logged odds of \(y=1\) increase at a constant rate.

X Probability of y = 1 Odds of y = 1 logged odds of y = 1
1 0.06 0.06/0.94 = 0.06 -2.8
2 0.20 0.2/0.8 = 0.25 -1.4
3 0.50 0.5/0.5 = 1 0.0
4 0.80 0.8/0.2 = 4 1.4
5 0.94 0.94/0.06 = 16 2.8

Logistic Regression: motivation

So this:

\[ log(\frac{p}{1-p}) = \alpha + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2X_2 ... \]

Gives us a way to think about a linear effect of X on Y even when Y is dichotomous.

Logistic Regression: downsides

The downsides:

  1. We can’t calculate a best fit using least squares. We have to switch to an alternative method called “maximum likelihood estimation”. We also can’t calculate things like the R^2 value.
  1. Logit results are harder to interpret.

Interpreting Logistic Regression

Interpreting coefficients

Three things to remember:

  • logit coefficients represent the effects of a one unit change in “X” on the logged odds of Y = 1. No one thinks in terms of logged odds, so this is not very useful on its own.

  • Exponentiating (the inverse of logging) coefficients turns them into odds ratios. Odds ratios represent a multiplicative effect. So an exponentiated coefficient of 2 means each one-unit increase in X doubles the odds of Y=1

  • We can get predicted probabilities from a logit model, but the marginal effect of a change in X on the predicted probability of Y is not constant in additive or multiplicative terms. So there’s no single “effect” on the probability scale.

Interpreting coefficients

Lets go back to the turnout model. (We’ll just focus on the coefficients for now and ignore p.values)

Here’s the original linear probability model.

Code 
turnout_model_1<-regC(turnout_dummy ~ bachelors_or_more, 
                     data=nes,
                     w=wt) 
turnout_model_1

The direction of the coefficients are the same, but otherwise, these are totally different models. The logit coefficients no longer directly correspond to a probability.

Interpreting coefficients

  • Right now the coefficients represent the effect of a one-unit change in the log-odds of voting, but that’s not exactly intuitive.

  • We do know that positive values indicate positive effects, negative values indicate negative effects, and large values indicate stronger relationships. But that’s about it for the moment.

Odds ratios

  • Odds ratios represent a multiplicative effect. So 3.4 means that having a Bachelor’s is associated with a 3.4 fold increase in the odds of turnout.
  • The odds of voting if person has a Bachelor’s degree will be 3.4 times higher compared to a person without one.
  • The exponentiated intercept term represents the odds of voting for those without a degree

orci(turnout_logit_1)

Getting a probability

We can convert the intercept back into a probability by taking \(\text{odds} / (1 + \text{odds})\)

  • So \(3.78/(1+3.78) \approx .79\)

To get the probability of voting if someone has a Bachelor’s degree, we would need to multiply the odds ratios before converting them to a probability.

  • \(3.78 \times 3.42 \approx 12.9\) and \(12.9/(1+12.9) = .93\)

Getting a probability

To get a predicted probability, we could take the “linear prediction” and then convert the whole thing back to a probability.

The linear predictors are what we get from plugging each coefficient and value in to the linear model formula:

\[ \text{linpred} = \alpha + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2... \]

We can convert it back to a probability with this formula:

\[ \frac{e^{\text{linpred}}}{1+e^\text{linpred}} \]

Getting a probability

# probability without a Bachelors:

linpred <- 1.33
p0 <-exp(linpred)/(1+exp(linpred))
p0
[1] 0.7908406
# probability with a Bachelors:
linpred <- 1.33 + 1.23
p1<-exp(linpred) / (1 + exp(linpred))
p1
[1] 0.9282425
# effect of Bachelor's degrees on the 
# probability of turnout
p1 - p0
[1] 0.1374018

Logit with two or more variables

Logit with two or more variables

When we have a single binary independent variable, the logit model and linear probability model are basically interchangeable.

Logit is useful, though, when we go back to our more complicated model that includes an additional IV for political knowledge.

Step 1: Get the linear prediction by treating this like a normal regression model:

\[ \text{linpred} = -0.26 + 0.72 + 0.36 \times {10} = 4.06 \]

Step 2: Use the inverse logit function \(\frac{e^{\text{linpred}}}{1+e^\text{linpred}}\) to convert this back to a probability

exp(4.06) /(1 +  exp(4.06))
[1] 0.9830435

Predicted Probabilities: with the predict function

If we’ve saved our model, we can do all the math here with the predict.glm function with the response=TRUE option

# estimate the model and assign the result to a named object
turnout_mod<-logregC(turnout_dummy ~ bachelors_or_more + polquiz.index, 
                     data=nes,
                     w=wt)
# create a data frame with your hypothetical scenario
scenario <- data.frame(bachelors_or_more = 1, polquiz.index =10)
# get the prediction for this model and this scenario:
predict.glm(turnout_mod, newdata  = scenario, type='response')
        1 
0.9821815

Predicted Probabilities: with the predict function

We can also get predictions for several groups at once. (Notice we don’t get straight lines here!)

# all values of political knowledge test
polquiz_values <- 0:10

# predictions for Bachelor's
bs_or_more <- predict.glm(
  turnout_mod,
  type = 'response',
  newdata  = data.frame(bachelors_or_more = 1, 
                        polquiz.index = polquiz_values)
  
)
# predictions for No Bachelor's
less_than_bs <- predict.glm(
  turnout_mod,
  type = 'response',
  newdata  = data.frame(bachelors_or_more = 0, 
                        polquiz.index = polquiz_values)
)

# plot results
plot(x =polquiz_values, 
     type = 'n',
     ylim = c(.4, 1),
     xlab = 'Polquiz Index',
     ylab = 'Pr(Turnout=1)'
     )

# line for bachelor's
lines(x = polquiz_values, y = bs_or_more, 
      col='blue', lty=3)
# line for no bachelor's
lines(x = polquiz_values, y = less_than_bs, 
      col='black', lty=1)
                       
legend("bottomright", lty=c(3,1), bty="n",
legend=c("Has Bachelor's", "No degree"))
